stories.title: Sneak Peek: The New Train Linking Singapore and Johor Bahru
stories.headline_kid: Reporters got a first look at the new train station that will let you zip from Singapore to Johor Bahru in minutes!
summary: Right now, if you want to go from Singapore to Johor Bahru, you usually take a bus or car across the Causeway, and it can take a long, long time because of traffic jams. Soon, there will be a much faster way: a special train called the RTS Link, connecting Woodlands North MRT station in Singapore to a brand-new station called Bukit Chagar in Johor Bahru.

Reporters were recently allowed inside Bukit Chagar station before it opens. They saw high-tech body scanners (like the ones at airports) to keep passengers safe, and 'e-gates' where a machine checks your passport automatically instead of a person stamping it by hand. The station even has a direct walkway straight into nearby shopping malls, so you won't need to walk far in the hot sun.

Malaysia's transport planners are hoping the whole trip — leaving your house, going through both countries' checks, and arriving at your destination — could take as little as 25 minutes for many commuters. That would be a huge time-saver compared to today's long queues.

The RTS Link is expected to open in January 2027. Many families who shop, eat or work across the border are excited, because it means less time stuck in traffic and more time doing fun things (or just getting home for dinner faster)!

lenses.me: If your family likes trips to Johor Bahru for food or shopping, this train could make your weekend outings much quicker and easier.
lenses.family: Parents who currently dread the long Causeway jam might soon choose the train instead, saving time and stress.
lenses.friends: Classmates whose parents work in Johor Bahru might talk about shorter commutes for their families once this opens.
lenses.nation: The RTS Link shows how closely Singapore and Malaysia work together to solve problems like traffic and improve daily life for both countries.
lenses.world: It's an example of how neighbouring countries can build shared infrastructure to make travel easier for everyone.

stories.title: Would You Pay $700 to Live in a Storeroom?
stories.headline_kid: Because rents in Singapore are so high, some people are choosing to live in tiny rooms that used to be storerooms!
summary: Renting a home in Singapore can be very expensive these days. To save money, some tenants are giving up having a big room, and instead renting very small spaces — sometimes rooms that used to be used just for storing things, not for sleeping in.
One man in the news, Mr Jao Santos, rents a tiny room like this. It's small, but it's in a good location close to where he needs to be, and it costs much less than a normal-sized room nearby.

This shows a trade-off many people in Singapore are making: choosing a smaller space in exchange for saving money or being close to work, school or transport. It's a bit like choosing a smaller slice of cake if it means you get to eat it sooner and closer to home!

This story is part of a bigger issue — rental prices in Singapore have been rising, making it harder for some people to afford comfortable living spaces. It reminds us how important it is to plan and budget carefully.

lenses.me: It helps you understand that sometimes people make trade-offs, choosing less space to save money — similar to choosing a smaller toy to save your pocket money for something else.
lenses.family: Your family might discuss how housing costs affect decisions about where to live or how much to spend on rent.
lenses.friends: Some of your friends' families might also be affected by rising rents, even if they don't talk about it much.
lenses.nation: This highlights a real challenge in Singapore — making sure housing stays affordable for everyone, not just the wealthy.
lenses.world: Many big cities around the world face similar problems with expensive rent and shrinking living spaces.

stories.title: A Mystery Website Trying to Trick Singapore's Diplomats
stories.headline_kid: A fake company pretending to be from Singapore is trying to hire people who used to work for our government!
summary: CNA reporters found a suspicious website for a company called 'Great Vision', which claims to be a consulting firm based in Singapore. But when investigators looked closer, they found things that didn't add up — including a false claim that its boss used to be a real Singapore diplomat (someone who represents our country to the world).

This is one of nine suspicious websites that CNA has been investigating recently. What makes Great Vision different is that it's the first one caught specifically trying to recruit people who used to work for Singapore's Ministry of Foreign Affairs or related think tanks.

Why does this matter? Think of it like a stranger pretending to be your friend's cousin just to get information about your family. Fake companies like this might be trying to gather secrets or influence people who know how our government works, which could be risky for Singapore's safety and reputation.
Authorities are looking into this. It's a good reminder for everyone — even grown-ups — to always check if a company or job offer is real before trusting it, especially online.

lenses.me: It teaches you to be careful about strangers online, just like being careful about strangers in real life.
lenses.family: Parents and older family members should double-check any surprising job offers, even ones that sound impressive.
lenses.friends: You and your friends can talk about staying safe online and not trusting things just because they look official.
lenses.nation: This protects Singapore's important government information and keeps our country's reputation trustworthy.
lenses.world: It's part of a bigger global problem of fake websites and disguised attempts to gather secret information.

stories.title: Malaysia Airlines Tests All Its Pilots for Drugs
stories.headline_kid: After a pilot was caught with a huge amount of illegal drugs, the whole airline checked every pilot — and good news, they all passed!
summary: On July 28, a Malaysia Airlines pilot was arrested in Jakarta, Indonesia, after officials found 26kg of MDMA — a dangerous, mind-altering drug — hidden in his luggage. That's a shockingly large amount, roughly as heavy as a big bag of rice!

Because of this scary discovery, Malaysia Airlines decided to test all of its pilots for drugs, to make sure everyone flying their planes is safe and alert. Pilots need clear minds because they're responsible for hundreds of passengers' lives.
The good news: every single pilot tested negative, meaning no drugs were found in anyone else. The airline is now moving on to test its cabin crew (the flight attendants who help passengers) as well.
This matters to Singaporeans too, since many of us fly Malaysia Airlines to Kuala Lumpur or beyond. Strict safety checks like this help make sure flights stay safe for everyone on board.

lenses.me: It shows why grown-ups in important jobs, like pilots, must always stay alert and follow strict rules.
lenses.family: If your family flies Malaysia Airlines, this news might make them feel reassured about safety.
lenses.friends: You could chat with friends about what other jobs need extra-strict safety rules, like bus drivers or doctors.
lenses.nation: Singapore and Malaysia are close neighbours, and many Singaporeans travel using Malaysian airlines, so this safety news affects us directly.
lenses.world: It reminds airlines everywhere how important it is to keep drug-free, alert crews for passenger safety.

stories.title: A Blocked Sea Path Is Making Oil More Expensive Again
stories.headline_kid: A narrow sea passage is still causing trouble, pushing up oil prices around the world — and that could affect prices here in Singapore too.
summary: The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow strip of sea near Iran that huge ships use to carry oil to countries all over the world. Think of it like a single doorway that a lot of important cargo must pass through — if the doorway gets stuck, everything behind it gets delayed.

The US and Iran have been in a tense stand-off for months, and a ceasefire deadline between them passed on Monday without any deal to reopen the strait properly. Because of this uncertainty, oil prices have been climbing higher.

When oil becomes more expensive, it doesn't just affect big companies — it can also make petrol, bus and taxi rides, and even everyday items pricier, because almost everything needs energy to be made or transported. On top of this, stock markets in America fell too, as investors grew worried about the unclear situation.

Singapore doesn't have its own oil, so we import nearly all our energy. This means we keep a close eye on situations like this, since rising oil prices overseas can eventually be felt in our own wallets, from petrol pumps to grocery bills.

lenses.me: If oil prices go up, things like Grab rides or bus fares might slowly become more expensive too.
lenses.family: Your family's petrol bills, groceries, or transport costs could be affected if this situation continues.
lenses.friends: You and your friends might notice adults talking more about rising prices at home or on the news.
lenses.nation: Since Singapore imports all its energy, this kind of global tension can directly affect our cost of living.
lenses.world: It shows how one small but important sea passage can affect prices and economies everywhere, proving how connected our world really is.
